synopsis: DOE is strongest for estimating how factors and low-order interactions affect detection distance, stopping margin and false alarms; screening identifies influential factors, while response-surface designs support fine tuning of a few smooth parameters [f6799, f6805, f6801, f6673]. The booklet places modest DOE or D-optimal tests in post-prototype calibration, and recommends sequential braking-model experiments whose stopping criterion is sufficiently small safety-relevant error bounds at every declared operating boundary—not a fixed test count [f14109, f14504, f6166, f6169]. DOE points are not weighted by operational frequency, so they cannot establish field failure probability; fractional designs also alias higher-order effects and cannot rule out narrow, nonlinear failures between test points [f6807, f6800, f6808, f6809]. NIST software research reports equivalent fault detection with test sets reduced by factors of 20–700, but this does not demonstrate that pairwise or other low-order coverage suffices for off-road collision avoidance or coupled perception failures [f6820, f4075, f7425]. No off-road collision-avoidance study using DOE was found, and NIOSH's 2022 review identifies DOE and standard simulation-method gaps that additional synthetic runs do not close [f6812, f10508].
